lines.text: Say the color of this word. Not the word. The color.
lines.headline: Say the ink color, *not the word.*

lines.text: In 1935, psychologist John Ridley Stroop timed a hundred college students doing exactly this.
lines.headline: *Stroop,* 1935

lines.text: Naming the colors of plain squares took about sixty-three seconds.
lines.headline: The clash ==costs time.==

lines.text: When the ink fought the word, it took a hundred and ten. About seventy-four percent longer.
Reading is so practiced, it happens automatically.
lines.headline: Reading *wins the race.*

lines.text: Your brain has to brake that habit before it can answer.
When a strong habit shouts the wrong answer, pause for one beat, and check.
Save this, and try it on a friend.

post.title: Say the Color, Not the Word (Your Brain Will Stall) #shorts
post.description: The Stroop effect: in 1935 J. Ridley Stroop found that naming the ink color of a clashing color word took about 74% longer than naming plain color squares (about 110 s vs 63 s per sheet). Reading is automatic, so your brain has to brake it first. Stroop, J. R. (1935). Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 18, 643-662. #psychology #shorts #brain #stroopeffect
